With respect to CNS penetrance, while direct quantification of CNS drug levels is difficult, several lines of
evidence support CNS delivery of H74DS3M8 in vivo. The compound is based on the same hydroxyl dendrimer
scaffold (and shares the same biophysical delivery) as our 18F-FMD PET tracer (14.462 kDa vs. 20.320 kDa for
H74DS3M8), which successfully crossed the BBB and selectively accumulated in regions of neuroinflammation,
as shown in our imaging data in Figures 2-5. Importantly, H74DS3M8 was administered at a substantially higher
mass dose (micromolar vs. nanomolar), increasing the likelihood of CNS uptake.
Furthermore, the EAE model used in this study is characterized by BBB disruption, which enhances CNS
penetration of systemically administered agents. This mirrors well-documented BBB dysfunction observed in
human MS, particularly during active lesions. Numerous studies using gadolinium-enhanced MRI, histology,
and molecular markers have confirmed BBB leakage in MS patients during both relapsing and progressive
phases (Lassmann et al., Nat Rev Neurol 2012; Minagar & Alexander, Neurochem Res 2003). Activated myeloid
cells and reactive endothelial changes further promote permeability in both the EAE model and human disease.
Given the shared dendrimer architecture, the higher dosing of H74DS3M8, and the presence of BBB dysfunction
in EAE and human MS, we believe it is reasonable to conclude that H74DS3M8 reaches the CNS where it can
then have its desired effect on its target myeloid cell populations. Together, these factors support the
interpretation that the observed therapeutic effects are due to on-target modulation of CNS immune activity.
We have added the following text to the results section:
“H74DS3M8 is a hydroxyl dendrimer conjugated with eight novel dasatinib payloads, engineered to selectively
target activated myeloid cells via fluid-phase endocytosis and inhibit CSF1R with high potency. Kinase profiling
revealed sub-nanomolar potency against CSF1R, ABL1, c-Kit, and c-Src, with minimal off-target activity against
EGFR and PDGFRβ (Supplementary Table 3). In cell-based assays, H74DS3M8 inhibited proliferation in BV2
microglial cells in a dose-dependent manner, with an IC of 343 nM at 52 hours (Supplementary Fig. 1).
mechanism of action of H74DS3M8 from other CSF1R inhibitors whose primary mechanism is through microglial
killing or depletion. Pharmacokinetic studies demonstrated sustained systemic exposure following both
intraperitoneal (i.p.) and intravenous administration, supporting its suitability for in vivo applications
(Supplementary Table 4). Noncompartmental analysis of sparse-sampling data revealed log-linear elimination
kinetics with terminal plasma half-lives (HL_Lambda_z) of 3.44 hours (i.p.) and 3.15 hours (i.v.), respectively
(Supplementary Fig. 2), consistent with a clearance profile appropriate for therapeutic targeting of CNS
inflammation.“
Comment 6:
Overlapping author affiliations with Ashvattha Therapeutics: Several authors are affiliated with the company
developing both 18F-FMD and H74DS3M8, creating a potential conflict of interest that may influence the
interpretation of results.
Response: Thank you for your comment. This study was sponsored by Ashvattha Therapeutics; however, all
experiments, data analysis, and interpretation were independently led and conducted by our research team at
Stanford. We have fully disclosed all author affiliations and potential conflicts of interest in the manuscript to
ensure transparency. While the study design and analyses were discussed with Ashvattha, they did not influence

Comment 7:
I would suggest the authors address these concerns with additional experiments and resubmit a more
comprehensive manuscript with expanded controls and improved statistical rigor.
Response: Thank you for raising these very helpful comments. We have addressed all concerns by performing
additional experiments to strengthen the manuscript. Specifically, we expanded the control groups where
appropriate, increased the sample size to at least n=5 in all treatment response studies to improve statistical
rigor, and revised the relevant text and figures accordingly. We believe these revisions significantly enhance the

mice after immunomodulatory therapy
Response to Reviewers’ Comments:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
General comments:
I greatly appreciate that the authors have effectively addressed the issues I raised in my previous review,
performing new analyses and updating their figures and results accordingly.
However, a couple of important issues remain to be addressed:
Comment 1:
Regarding the response to comment 2: The authors state that it is not possible to include post-mortem data from
progressive MS patients due to the biophysical mechanisms of PET tracer uptake. In this case, it is essential to
clearly state in the limitations section of the manuscript that, as it currently stands, the presented results do not
demonstrate the utility of this novel tracer in the context of progressive MS. Any such utility can only be
hypothesized at this stage.
Response: Thank you so much for this very helpful comment. We agree that this is an important limitation and
have added a paragraph to the discussion section to address this point.
The following text has been added to the discussion section:
“Another important limitation is that, due to the biophysical mechanism of uptake of our PET tracer via fluid-
phase endocytosis by activated myeloid cells, it is not possible to evaluate 18F-FMD specificity or uptake patterns
in vitro using post-mortem tissue sections. Both the Cy5- and 18F-labeled dendrimer conjugates require living,
metabolically active cells for internalization, and endocytic activity ceases upon cell death. Consequently,
analyses of these agents in fresh-frozen or fixed MS tissues are not possible.”
Comment 2:
Regarding the response to comment 3: I appreciate that the authors have included a reference to the revised
implication—that this novel tracer could enable a more accurate or earlier diagnosis of MS is not supported by
the presented data and should be removed from all sections of the manuscript. For instance, statements such
as “These preclinical results highlight the potential utility of 18F-FMD in a clinical setting, particularly as the field
moves toward earlier diagnosis of MS,” or “However, diagnostic uncertainty remains a challenge in cases with
ambiguous radiographic or clinical presentations,” imply that the novel PET tracer may help resolve diagnostic
uncertainty. However, this implication is not supported by the presented data, nor is it plausible even as a
theoretical hypothesis based on the current evidence. Therefore, any reference of the new tracer having a
potential to allow an earlier or more accurate diagnosis of MS have to be removed from the manuscript.
Instead, the authors could emphasize that while conventional MRI is widely and effectively used both to diagnose
MS and to monitor treatment efficacy, it lacks specificity for innate immune cells—cells known to play a key role
in the neurodegenerative aspects of MS pathology. Furthermore, as new treatments are being developed that
specifically target innate immune cells, there is a growing need for advanced imaging techniques capable of
evaluating the efficacy of these therapies. In this context, the novel tracer may fill an important gap, representing
a promising method to specifically image pro-inflammatory innate immune cell activity in the brains of people
with MS.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important clarification. We have carefully removed all statements
suggesting that this tracer may contribute to earlier or more accurate MS diagnosis. The revised text now
emphasizes the established role of conventional MRI for diagnosis and monitoring, while highlighting that its
limitation lies in the lack of specificity for innate immune cells. We further revised the discussion to underscore
that 18F-FMD PET is positioned not as a diagnostic tool, but rather as a complementary approach with potential
utility in evaluating therapeutic responses and monitoring innate immune dynamics, particularly as new
treatments targeting these cell populations are being developed.
The following text has been modified in the discussion section:
“Conventional MRI remains the cornerstone of MS care, serving as the primary tool for both diagnosis and
longitudinal monitoring of treatment efficacy. The revised McDonald criteria, introduced at the 40th Congress of
the European Committee for Treatment and Research in Multiple Sclerosis (ECTRIMS) in 2024, have further
expanded the role of clinical and imaging parameters, reinforcing the central role of structural MRI in facilitating
more timely diagnoses61. However, while MRI provides critical structural information, it lacks specificity for innate
immune cells–cell populations increasingly recognized as key drivers of the neurodegenerative aspects of MS
pathology. As new therapeutic strategies emerge that target these cells directly, there is a growing need for
advanced imaging approaches capable of capturing their dynamics and treatment responses in vivo. In this
context, 18F-FMD PET has the potential to offer a complementary approach by enabling cell-specific, real-time
visualization of innate immune activation. Herein, we demonstrated that 18F-FMD PET sensitively detected
reductions in CNS inflammatory activity in EAE mice following treatment with either FTY720, an FDA-approved
S1P receptor modulator, or H74DS3M8, a novel CSF1R-targeting dendranib. These reductions were
corroborated by flow cytometry and ex vivo analyses, underscoring the tracer’s ability to track immune
modulation with high specificity. Together, these results support 18F-FMD PET as a promising biomarker for
monitoring innate immune dynamics and therapeutic efficacy, complementing structural MRI and potentially
guiding the development and evaluation of emerging MS therapies.”
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
General comments:
The authors have sufficiently addressed my comments. The additions / modifications made, significantly
enhanced the manuscript. I have no additional comments.
Response: Thank you! We appreciate your thoughtful review and positive feedback.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
General comments:
This manuscript presents a technically rigorous evaluation of ¹⁸F-FMD as a PET tracer for detecting activated
myeloid cells in an EAE mouse model of multiple sclerosis. The authors employ multiple complementary
methodologies and demonstrate impressive technical expertise in radiotracer development, PET imaging, and
immunological characterization. The work addresses an important clinical need for biomarkers that can detect
neuroinflammation and monitor therapeutic responses in MS.
However, several fundamental limitations raise questions about the translational relevance of these findings:
Comment 1:
Model Limitations: The EAE model involves artificial immune activation using Complete Freund's Adjuvant and
pertussis toxin, creating what the authors acknowledge as "strong peripheral innate immune activation" that
"alters CNS-resident immune cell behavior." This artificial immune environment may not adequately represent
the pathophysiology of human MS, where disease initiation occurs through different mechanisms.
Response: Thank you for raising this critical point. We agree that the EAE model presented in this manuscript
involves artificial immune activation, and as such cannot fully recapitulate the pathophysiology of human MS.
We performed these EAE studies specifically to evaluate the performance of our tracer in a preclinical MS model
and to obtain proof-of-concept data showing that 18F-FMD can detect innate immune activation in mice with MS-
like symptoms and monitor therapeutic responses to two different therapies. These data strengthen the feasibility
and safety rationale for translation by demonstrating selective targeting of activated myeloid cells, favorable
pharmacokinetics, and the ability to measure therapeutic modulation in vivo.
Our major objective was to move into human studies as quickly as possible. Excitingly, this tracer is currently
being evaluated in a phase 1/2 clinical trial (NCT05395624). Our goal is to image as many MS patients as
possible, including individuals across the spectrum of MS subtypes, to rigorously establish clinical utility. We also
recognize that all animal models fall short in fully capturing human disease complexity; thus, our preclinical data
are not intended to be directly translationally definitive but rather serve as an essential bridge enabling us to
advance safely and rationally into studies in people.
The following texts have been modified in the discussion section:
“The induction of EAE via MOG peptide and Complete Freund’s adjuvant (CFA) is an artificial process that
35-55
does not naturally occur in human MS. CFA triggers strong peripheral innate immune activation to facilitate
antigen presentation, which in turn alters CNS-resident immune cell behavior80. This preclinical immune milieu
may therefore not adequately represent the pathophysiology of human MS, underscoring the need for clinical
studies to evaluate the performance of 18F-FMD.”
“This trial aims to validate the sensitivity, specificity, and uptake patterns of 18F-FMD in patients, and to establish
whether they mirror those observed in preclinical models. In addition, the study will evaluate the tracer’s utility
for monitoring neuroinflammatory activity, assessing treatment response, and enabling patient stratification in
clinical settings.”
Comment 2:
Blood-Brain Barrier Considerations: The authors acknowledge that EAE involves BBB disruption, which may
facilitate tracer access to CNS parenchyma. While they argue that selective uptake depends on endocytic activity
rather than passive leakage, this mechanism has not been validated under conditions of intact BBB function.
Human MS exhibits more heterogeneous and potentially less extensive BBB compromise, raising questions
about tracer performance in clinical settings.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important comment. We agree that this is a major consideration when
interpreting our results. The EAE model involves BBB disruption, and translation into the clinical context will
require consideration of the heterogeneity and varying extent of BBB compromise across different stages of MS.
While our tracer uptake depends on endocytic activity rather than passive leakage, we acknowledge that BBB
integrity may influence performance under conditions of more limited or heterogeneous barrier disruption.
Accordingly, we have revised the limitation paragraph in our discussion to explicitly highlight BBB heterogeneity
in human MS:
“Furthermore, BBB disruption in human MS is more heterogenous and typically less pronounced than in EAE,
complicating direct extrapolation from animal models. Definitive evaluation of tracer uptake patterns will therefore
require clinical validation, where the interplay of BBB integrity, immune activation, and disease heterogeneity
can be directly assessed.”
At this time, we cannot fully know how our approach will perform in the setting of intact or partially compromised
BBB until clinical studies are completed. We have therefore added a sentence to the limitations paragraph of the
manuscript to alert readers to this caveat. We consider this a key issue for evaluation and agree that human
studies will ultimately be required to address it directly. Importantly, we are actively investigating this question in
our ongoing clinical trial (NCT05395624; preliminary data published in Moradi, F. et al. J. Nucl. Med. 66, 251092
[2025]; reference 77). Our goal is to understand how 18F-FMD performs across the full spectrum of MS subtypes
(including RRMS, PPMS, SPMS, and PRMS) to establish its clinical utility in patients, where BBB compromise
is heterogenous and variable over time.
[77] Moradi, F. et al. [18F]Flurimedrimer, a Novel Nanomedicine Radiotracer, Selectively Targeting Activated
Microglia in Human Brain. J. Nucl. Med. 66, 251092 (2025).
Comment 3:
Species Translation Gap: The substantial differences between murine and human immune systems, particularly
regarding microglial activation patterns and myeloid cell responses, create uncertainty about cross-species
applicability. The behavior of the 14.5kDa dendrimer may differ significantly in human physiology.
Response: Thank you for raising this critical consideration. We agree that cross-species differences in microglial
and myeloid biology are a major consideration. Importantly, the hydroxyl-terminated PAMAM dendrimer platform
(the ~14.5 kDa scaffold used in 18F-FMD) has been evaluated in humans as OP-101 (dendrimer-N-
acetylcysteine). In a multicenter, randomized, double-blind phase 2a trial in adults with severe COVID-19, single-
dose intravenous OP-101 was well tolerated, reduced systemic inflammation, and lowered neurological injury
markers (NfL and GFAP) versus placebo – consistent with selective delivery to activated macrophage/microglia-
lineage cells in vivo (Gusdon et al. Sci Transl Med. 2022 Jul 20;14(654):eabo2652). These data provide direct
human evidence that this hydroxyl dendrimer platform behaves safely and with the intended immune-cell-
targeting pharmacology in an inflammatory clinical setting.
In addition, the in vivo pharmacology of hydroxyl dendrimers has been extensively validated in more than 30
animal models of neuroinflammation, including non-human primate and canine models (Kannan 2012; Kannan
2014; Mishra 2014; Nance 2015; Guo 2016; Nance 2016; Zhang 2016; Nance 2017; Niño 2018; Turk 2018;
Liaw 2020; Sharma 2020; Cabeza 2021; Henningfield 2024). Across these studies, hydroxyl dendrimers consistently
cross the BBB in the presence of neuroinflammation, distribute rapidly after systemic administration, and are
selectively internalized by activated macrophages and microglia in proportion to disease severity. Notably,
Henningfield et al. (Alzheimers Res Ther. 2024 May 6;16(1):101) showed that Cy5-labeled hydroxyl dendrimers
preferentially accumulated in plaque-associated microglia in 5xFAD mice. The 5xFAD model is characterized by
a comparatively intact BBB, with only localized and age-dependent permeability changes, underscoring that
dendrimer uptake in this setting reflects genuine cellular targeting rather than nonspecific paracellular leakage.
Finally, large-animal studies reported by other groups provide additional confidence in translational applicability.
In non-human primates with ischemic optic neuropathy and in canines subjected to hypothermic circulatory arrest,
hydroxyl dendrimers selectively trafficked to injured CNS tissue and glia while showing negligible uptake in
uninvolved regions (Guo et al. PLoS One. 2016 Apr 29;11(4):e0154437; Mishra et al. ACS Nano. 2014 Mar
25;8(3):2134-47). These findings suggest preservation of the dendrimer’s CNS trafficking and targeting
mechanisms across species.
Taken together, the convergence of direct human trial data with OP-101, consistent findings across small- and
large-animal neuroinflammatory models, and mechanistic studies showing selective uptake by activated
microglia and macrophages provide strong evidence that the pharmacology of hydroxyl dendrimers is conserved
across species. The aim of our current study is to establish in vivo tracer specificity and pharmacology in a well-
characterized preclinical MS model as a bridge to clinical imaging. Building on the human OP-101 results and
large-animal evidence above, we are now evaluating 18F-FMD across all clinical MS subtypes to directly quantify
tracer performance in human physiology.
Comment 4:
Limited Disease Modeling: Testing in only one MS model (MOG35-55 EAE) provides insufficient evidence for
broader applicability. Human MS encompasses diverse subtypes with varying inflammatory profiles that may not
be adequately represented by this single model.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. We acknowledge that there are multiple preclinical models
of MS, each of which captures different aspects of disease biology. However, the goal of this study was not to
test tracer performance across a wide range of models, but rather to understand how our tracer performs in vivo
in a model that develops both neuroinflammation and lesions. Using the MOG EAE model allowed us to
35-55
assess the tracer’s uptake, biodistribution, and specificity in the context of acute neuroinflammation, thereby
providing essential information about the sensitivity and specificity of this imaging approach in vivo.
Since no single mouse model can fully recapitulate the pathophysiology or heterogeneity of human MS, our
ultimate goal was to move into clinical studies which are currently ongoing (NCT05395624), where the tracer is
being evaluated directly in patients across the full spectrum of MS subtypes. As such, the EAE experiments were
designed as a necessary preclinical step to establish feasibility and inform translation, rather than to exhaustively
model the diversity of MS disease presentations in animals.
Comment 5:
Ethical Considerations: The extensive use of animals (160 mice) subjected to neurological disease with paralysis
as endpoints appears disproportionate given the uncertain translational value. The authors have not
demonstrated that alternative research approaches (human tissue studies, computational modeling, existing
clinical data) were adequately explored before conducting this extensive animal study.
Response: We appreciate this important point and agree that ethical considerations are central in animal
research. Alternative approaches, however, are not feasible for the aims of this study. The goal of our work was
to assess the uptake, biodistribution, and specificity of 18F-FMD in vivo. At present, there are no available
computational models or in vitro techniques capable of recapitulating the complex in vivo behavior of radiotracers,
including their stability, kinetics, biodistribution, specificity, and non-specific binding. While computational
modeling has shown promise in drug discovery, predictive modeling for PET tracer performance remains limited,
and we are actively exploring this area in our lab.
In addition, the biophysical mechanism of uptake for 18F-FMD (via fluid-phase endocytosis by activated myeloid
cells) cannot be meaningfully reproduced in tissue sections or static in vitro systems as these cannot replicate
the dynamic cell-environment interactions present in living organisms. New PET radiotracers must undergo
evaluation in rodents and/or large animas (e.g., non-human primates) as a critical step before human studies.
We would also like to emphasize that the number of mice used was carefully justified. All experiments were
designed a priori to achieve appropriate statistical power; we used the minimum number of animals necessary
to rigorously test our hypotheses across multiple treatment arms and confirmatory analyses. Although 160 mice
were used in total, they were essential to establish the feasibility and safety rationale for moving into humans.
Finally, we note that this tracer is currently being evaluated in a phase 1/2 clinical trial (NCT05395624). These
animal studies were not conducted in isolation but rather as an ethically justified bridge, designed to provide the
proof-of-concept data necessary to support safe, rational translation into people. Our goal is to image as many
MS patients as possible to rigorously establish clinical utility.
Comment 6:
How do the authors address potential partial volume effects from renal clearance affecting spinal cord
quantification in such small anatomical structures?
Response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point and apologize for not explaining this more
clearly in the discussion section. To clarify, we addressed the potential issue for partial volume effects from renal
clearance impacting spinal quantification through two different ex vivo approaches: gamma counting and
autoradiography. To further explain these processes, spinal cords and kidneys were carefully dissected out of
each mouse following cardiac perfusion to remove any potential contributions of tracer signal in blood. For
gamma counting, the tissues were weighed wet, transferred into separate gamma counting tubes, and measured
using a gamma counter to obtain absolute quantitation of tracer concentration in individual organs, normalized
to weight. This technique allows us to determine absolute tracer concentrations in each tissue without any
potential for spillover or partial volume effects that can occur in PET imaging. To further understand the tracer
uptake pattern (with higher resolution) in spinal cords, we embedded them in OCT, cryosectioned into thin (60
µm) slices, and exposed on digital phosphorous films to obtain high-resolution spatial distribution data. These
ex vivo analyses, performed independently of the in vivo PET data, confirmed that tracer uptake within the spinal
cord reflected true biological signal and was not artifactual due to renal clearance or blood pool signal or any
other partial volume effects. Together, these complementary methods strengthen the robustness of our
quantification and provide confidence in the specificity of our findings.
The following text has been modified in the discussion section:
“Given the renal clearance of 18F-FMD and the small size of EAE mice, there is a possibility of partial volume
effects from adjacent kidneys affecting signal quantification in the lumbar spinal cord. Partial volume corrections
using post-reconstruction- and reconstruction-based methods could help circumvent this limitation73. However,
these correction techniques are challenging to implement effectively in mouse models due to the extremely small
size and thin geometry of the spinal cord, which often falls below the spatial resolution of small-animal PET
scanners74,75. This leads to significant spillover and underestimation of true activity even after correction,
particularly when adjacent high-uptake organs like kidneys are involved. Instead, we mitigated this issue by
dissecting the kidneys and spinal cord out of each mouse for gamma counting and performed autoradiography
on thin spinal cord sections. These techniques eliminate contributions from circulating tracer and provide higher
sensitivity and spatial resolution respectively, without any possibility for spillover from adjacent tissues.
Using
these methods, we observed a dramatic elevation in spinal cord signal in EAE mice compared to naïve controls,
corroborating in vivo PET findings. Importantly, this limitation is less relevant in larger species, such as non-
human primates or humans, where the increased anatomical separation between kidneys and spinal cord
reduces the likelihood of signal interference, allowing for more accurate delineation of regions of interest.”
Comment 7:
Could the authors provide additional validation using models with intact blood-brain barriers to confirm specificity
mechanisms?
Response: Thank you so much for this comment. We fully agree that confirming the specificity of the mechanism
of tracer uptake is important. As mentioned in our manuscript, 18F-FMD does not accumulate in healthy CNS
tissues, but only accumulates in regions containing neuroinflammation, where it is selectively endocytosed by
activated myeloid cells. We understand your concern regarding whether the uptake of our tracer depends
primarily on BBB disruption, and that it would be ideal to test in a model with an intact BBB. As you know,
microglial activation is closely linked to BBB function. Once there are activated myeloid cells present in the CNS,
they release cytokines, chemokines, and reactive oxygen species (among other mediators) that modulate
endothelial cells and pericytes. These chemical signals can subtly (or overtly) alter tight junction integrity,
endothelial pathways, transporter activity, and thus passage of PET tracers into and out of the CNS (Yoon et al.
Nat Commun 16, 699 (2025); Mayer and Fischer, Front Cell Neurosci. 2024 Mar 13;18:1360195; da Fonseca et
al. Front Cell Neurosci. 2014 Nov 3;8:362). It is thus challenging to identify a suitable model that contains our
target of interest (i.e., activated myeloid cells) in absence of BBB dysfunction.
We agree that EAE mice do indeed exhibit significant BBB compromise, and therefore you raise a valid question
about the specificity of the mechanism of uptake of our tracer. To address your concern, we have added
additional empirical data below validating the uptake of 18F-FMD in models with negligible BBB dysfunction.
Evidence of elevated 18F-FMD uptake in the cortex and hippocampus of 5xFAD mice at an early stage of
disease, known to have largely intact BBB (cited data; open access)
We evaluated 18F-FMD in the 5xFAD Alzheimer’s disease mouse model, which is known to have a largely intact
BBB before 4 months of age and only modestly altered between 4-8 months (Zhukov et al., Front Aging Neurosci.
5xFAD mice (Figure 1 and Table 1), which is an early stage of disease, 18F-FMD uptake was threefold higher in
cortex and hippocampus (regions with known AD pathology and microglial activation) compared to wild-type
controls, with higher sensitivity than TSPO-PET using 18F-GE180 (a small molecule that crosses the intact rodent
BBB and binds to the translocator protein 18kDa, a widely explored PET imaging biomarker of
neuroinflammation). This data provides strong evidence that the predominate mechanism of 18F-FMD uptake is
via endocytosis of activated microglia rather than passive diffusion across a compromised BBB alone.
Figure 1. Coronal view of representative 3.75-month-old 5xFAD transgenic and wild-type mouse brain PET
images (50-60 min p.i. summed) using either 18F-FMD or 18F-GE180, co-registered with CT images. Carlson et
al., Alzheimer's Dement. 2022, 18: e060700.
Table 1. Tracer signal in 5xFAD mice normalized to wild-type mice signal (equivalent to signal-to-background
ratios) in brain regions known to contain amyloid pathology and microglial activation in 5xFAD mice imaged with
either 18F-FMD or 18F-GE180 at 3.75 months old.
18F-FMD (n=4 WT, n=4 5xFAD) 18F-GE180 (n=4 WT, n=5 5xFAD)
Cortex 3.18 1.21
Hippocampus 3.05 1.24
Whole Brain 3.14 1.21
Complementary evidence from fluorescent dendrimer analog of 18F-FMD (cited data; open access)
Henningfield et al. (Alzheimers Res Ther. 2024 May 6;16(1):101) confirmed the specificity of the fourth-
generation polyamidoamine (PAMAM) hydroxyl dendrimer (same scaffold as 18F-FMD), showing that this Cy5-
labeled dendrimer was regionally and selectively phagocytosed by plaque-associated microglia (PAMs) in 7-
month-old 5xFAD brains (Figure 1c). Their work corroborated our in vivo PET imaging data in 5xFAD mice and
showed robust Cy5 signal around dense-core plaques (Amylo-Glo-positive) and co-localization to Iba1+ microglia
and CD68+ microglial lysosomes in hippocampus and samatosensory cortex. Wild-type mice, by contrast,
exhibited negligible Cy5 signal. Additionally, staining for astrocytes, neurons, and oligodendrocytes showed no
Cy5 signal associated with those cells in the subiculum or somatosensory cortex (Fig. 1m-q).
Figure 1c from Henningfield et al. (Alzheimers Res Ther. 2024 May 6;16(1):101) demonstrates co-localization
of Cy5-labeled hydroxyl dendrimers (red) with microglia (Iba1, green) and dense core plaques (Amylo-Glo, blue).
Figure 1m-q from Henningfield et al. showing G4 hydroxyl dendrimers are selectively endocytosed by plaque-
associated microglia in the subiculum (p) and somatosensory cortex (q) regions of 5xFAD brain with no uptake
by astrocytes (m, m1), neurons (n), oligodendrocytes (o, o1).
Additional validation across models with limited BBB disruption (from Carlson et al., with permission)
We have also previously published a study assessing 18F-FMD in an LPS model induced by intraperitoneal
injection of LPS (rather than intracerebroventricularly; Carlson et al., Mol Imaging Biol. 2023;25:1063-1072),
where BBB alterations are modest compared to the EAE model used in our current study. In LPS mice, we
demonstrated a correlation between whole-brain 18F-FMD uptake and murine sepsis score – with increasing
score relating to elevated levels of activated microglia (Figure 4c).
Figure 4c shows strong correlation between 18F-FMD whole brain signal and severity of sepsis symptoms using
murine sepsis score (MSS). Adapted from Carlson et al., “Development and Initial Assessment of [18F]OP-801:
a Novel Hydroxyl Dendrimer PET Tracer for Preclinical Imaging of Innate Immune Activation in the Whole Body
and Brain,” Molecular Imaging and Biology, 25, 1063-1072 (2023), Springer Nature. Permission obtained via
RightsLink.
Moreover, the mechanism of uptake and biodistribution of these hydroxyl dendrimers has been characterized
extensively in over 30 animal models of neuroinflammation across species (including rodent, canine, and primate
models) by other groups. In these studies, G4 dendrimers consistently accumulated at sites of injury or
neuroinflammation but not in healthy brain tissue (Kannan 2012; Kannan 2014; Mishra 2014; Nance 2015; Guo
2016; Nance 2016; Zhang 2016; Nance 2017; Niño 2018; Turk 2018; Henningfield 2020; Liaw 2020; Sharma
2020; Cabeza 2021).
Taken together, these data (in particular, the 5xFAD mouse data collected by our lab using 18F-FMD in addition
to 5xFAD data collected and published by a separate lab using the fluorescently labeled version of this same
dendrimer), along with extensive G4 dendrimer biodistribution studies in multiple species, provide strong
evidence that 18F-FMD can cross the BBB both under conditions of overt disruption (e.g., EAE) and, importantly,
in models with minimal impairment (e.g., early-stage 5xFAD and i.p. LPS). Crucially, tracer retention occurs only
in regions containing activated myeloid cells, thus indicating that the predominate mechanism of uptake and
retention is endocytosis by activated myeloid cells.
The following text has been modified in the introduction section to more clearly articulate the mechanism of
uptake of our tracer:
“Fourth-generation hydroxyl dendrimers have been demonstrated to penetrant regions of a dysfunctional–but
not healthy, intact–blood-brain barrier (BBB), where they are quickly and selectively taken up by activated
myeloid cells via fluid phase endocytosis, and rapidly cleared from tissue that does not contain these cells27–34.”
Mechanistic evidence of selective endocytosis of generation 4 hydroxyl dendrimers by activated myeloid
cells
We used a CSF1R inhibitor dendranib to selectively inhibit the activation and proliferation of myeloid cells in EAE
mice (to investigate the specificity of our tracer uptake). In vivo PET imaging, complemented by ex vivo gamma
counting and autoradiography, demonstrated significantly reduced 18F-FMD uptake in CNS regions with known
EAE pathology, including the medulla, cerebellum, pons, and both the cervical/thoracic and lumbar spinal cord
(Figures 4 and 5 in the manuscript). Flow cytometry with a fluorescent analog of 18F-FMD (Cy5-labeled G4
hydroxyl dendrimer; Cy5-HD) further confirmed selective endocytosis of hydroxyl dendrimers by activated
microglia and infiltrating myeloid cells. Notably, CSF1R dendranib treatment led to a marked reduction in Cy5-
HD+ activated microglia (46-fold) and infiltrating macrophages (19-fold).
Given the breath of preclinical validation already generated, and as the reviewer noted in comment 5, we believe
that additional rodent models would add limited translational value. Instead, our priority is to complete our current
human studies. In our ongoing clinical trial (NCT05395624; preliminary data published in Moradi, F. et al. J. Nucl.
Med., 2025, 66, 251092; reference 77), our goal is to understand how 18F-FMD performs across the full spectrum
of MS subtypes (including RRMS, PPMS, SPMS, and PRMS) to establish its clinical utility in patients, where
BBB compromise is heterogeneous and variable over time.
Comment 8:
What evidence supports the assumption that fluid-phase endocytosis rates in activated murine myeloid cells
accurately reflect those in human cells?
Response: We appreciate this thoughtful comment. While cross-species differences in endocytic activity are
indeed important to consider, there is direct evidence that fluid-phase endocytosis of hydroxyl dendrimers is
conserved across rodent and human cells and tissues.
First, Kambhampati et al. (Eur J Pharm Biopharm. 2015 Sep;95(Pt B):239-49) performed a side-by-side in vitro
characterization of hydroxyl dendrimer uptake and release kinetics in murine BV2 microglial cells and in human
retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. The study demonstrated highly consistent patterns of dendrimer
internalization, trafficking, and intracellular retention between the murine and human cell systems, supporting
conserved uptake mechanisms across species at the cellular level.
Second, Kambhampati et al. (J Control Release. 2021 Jul 10;335:527-540) provided in vivo confirmation in both
rodent and human tissues. In a rat model of choroidal neovascularization (CNV), hydroxyl dendrimers selectively
accumulated in activated myeloid and glial cells. Importantly, the same paper also demonstrated dendrimer
uptake in post-mortem human diabetic eyes, localizing to activated myeloid and glial populations. This direct
comparison across rat and human tissue provides strong evidence that the endocytic targeting behavior of
hydroxyl dendrimers is conserved across species, including in relevant human disease contexts.
Collectively, these studies help bridge the translational gap by showing that the fluid-phase endocytosis of
hydroxyl dendrimers by activated myeloid cells is not unique to murine systems but is also observed in human
cells. This supports the rationale for extrapolating from murine models to human applications in the context of
18F-FMD pharmacology.

### Reviewer 1

I greatly appreciate that the authors have effectively addressed the issues I raised in my previous review, performing new analyses and updating their figures and results accordingly.
However, a couple of important issues remain to be addressed:
1) Regarding the response to comment 2:
The authors state that it is not possible to include post-mortem data from progressive MS patients due to the biophysical mechanisms of PET tracer uptake. In this case, it is essential to clearly state in the limitations section of the manuscript that, as it currently stands, the presented results do not demonstrate the utility of this novel tracer in the context of progressive MS. Any such utility can only be hypothesized at this stage.
2) Regarding the response to comment 3:
I appreciate that the authors have included a reference to the revised 2024 McDonald criteria; however, I believe the main point of my comment was missed. The claim—or even the implication—that this novel tracer could enable a more accurate or earlier diagnosis of MS is not supported by the presented data and should be removed from all sections of the manuscript. For instance, statements such as “These preclinical results highlight the potential utility of 18F-FMD in a clinical setting, particularly as the field moves toward earlier diagnosis of MS,” or “However, diagnostic uncertainty remains a challenge in cases with ambiguous radiographic or clinical presentations,” imply that the novel PET tracer may help resolve diagnostic uncertainty. However, this implication is not supported by the presented data, nor is it plausible even as a theoretical hypothesis based on the current evidence. Therefore, any reference of the new tracer having a potential to allow an earlier or more accurate diagnosis of MS have to be removed from the manuscript.
Instead, the authors could emphasize that while conventional MRI is widely and effectively used both to diagnose MS and to monitor treatment efficacy, it lacks specificity for innate immune cells—cells known to play a key role in the neurodegenerative aspects of MS pathology. Furthermore, as new treatments are being developed that specifically target innate immune cells, there is a growing need for advanced imaging techniques capable of evaluating the efficacy of these therapies. In this context, the novel tracer may fill an important gap, representing a promising method to specifically image pro-inflammatory innate immune cell activity in the brains of people with MS.

### Reviewer 2

The authors have suffieciently addressed my comments. The additions / modifications made, significantly enhanced the manuscript. I have no additional comments.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents a technically rigorous evaluation of ¹⁸F-FMD as a PET tracer for detecting activated myeloid cells in an EAE mouse model of multiple sclerosis. The authors employ multiple complementary methodologies and demonstrate impressive technical expertise in radiotracer development, PET imaging, and immunological characterization. The work addresses an important clinical need for biomarkers that can detect neuroinflammation and monitor therapeutic responses in MS.
However, several fundamental limitations raise questions about the translational relevance of these findings:
Model Limitations: The EAE model involves artificial immune activation using Complete Freund's Adjuvant and pertussis toxin, creating what the authors acknowledge as "strong peripheral innate immune activation" that "alters CNS-resident immune cell behavior." This artificial immune environment may not adequately represent the pathophysiology of human MS, where disease initiation occurs through different mechanisms.
Blood-Brain Barrier Considerations: The authors acknowledge that EAE involves BBB disruption, which may facilitate tracer access to CNS parenchyma. While they argue that selective uptake depends on endocytic activity rather than passive leakage, this mechanism has not been validated under conditions of intact BBB function. Human MS exhibits more heterogeneous and potentially less extensive BBB compromise, raising questions about tracer performance in clinical settings.
Species Translation Gap: The substantial differences between murine and human immune systems, particularly regarding microglial activation patterns and myeloid cell responses, create uncertainty about cross-species applicability. The behavior of the 14.5kDa dendrimer may differ significantly in human physiology.
Limited Disease Modeling: Testing in only one MS model (MOG35-55 EAE) provides insufficient evidence for broader applicability. Human MS encompasses diverse subtypes with varying inflammatory profiles that may not be adequately represented by this single model.
Ethical Considerations: The extensive use of animals (160 mice) subjected to neurological disease with paralysis as endpoints appears disproportionate given the uncertain translational value. The authors have not demonstrated that alternative research approaches (human tissue studies, computational modeling, existing clinical data) were adequately explored before conducting this extensive animal study.
How do the authors address potential partial volume effects from renal clearance affecting spinal cord quantification in such small anatomical structures?
Could the authors provide additional validation using models with intact blood-brain barriers to confirm specificity mechanisms?
What evidence supports the assumption that fluid-phase endocytosis rates in activated murine myeloid cells accurately reflect those in human cells?

## Paper

## Abstract

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurodegenerative disease driven by infiltration of activated innate immune cells into the central nervous system (CNS). Current imaging approaches for diagnosing and monitoring disease progression rely on structural lesions and cannot directly assess innate immune activity. Here, we describe a dendrimer positron emission tomography (PET) tracer, 18F-flurimedrimer (18F-FMD), for non-invasive, longitudinal tracking of activated myeloid cells. In an experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) murine model, 18F-FMD specifically detects myeloid activation at presymptomatic and symptomatic stages, with PET signal correlating with disease severity. Moreover, 18F-FMD sensitively captures therapeutic response to fingolimod (FTY720) and a CSF1R dendranib (H74DS3M8), both of which suppress immune cell activation and attenuate disease severity. These findings highlight the potential of 18F-FMD PET for specific, real-time monitoring of innate immune responses, and the applicability of the dendrimer in clinical settings for monitoring therapeutic efficacy, advancing the development of personalized, myeloid-targeted strategies for MS.

---

## Introduction

Multiple sclerosis (MS) is the most prevalent chronic autoimmune disease of the central nervous system (CNS), affecting nearly 2.9 million people worldwide1. Characterized by inflammation, demyelination, and neurodegeneration, MS presents as a heterogeneous disease with clinical manifestations that vary significantly among individuals. Although its exact etiology is unclear, MS is driven by a complex interplay between the adaptive and innate immune systems. Within the adaptive immune response, autoreactive T and B cells are central to MS pathogenesis. Pro-inflammatory T helper 1 (Th1) and Th17 cell subsets secrete cytokines such as interleukin-17 (IL-17) and IL-21, promoting CNS infiltration and amplifying inflammation, while B cells contribute by producing autoantibodies and modulating T cell responses2,3. In parallel, the innate immune system – particularly myeloid cells including microglia, monocytes, macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells – plays a crucial role in both the progression and potential remission of MS4,5. Activated microglia and infiltrating macrophages are the predominant immune cell types found in acute and chronic active MS lesions within the CNS6–9. These cells drive neuroinflammation through the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, reactive oxygen species, and other neurotoxic mediators; they also phagocytose myelin and debris, and sustain lymphocyte activation through antigen presentation and cytokine polarization10–12. Notably, myeloid cell activation is present early in the disease course and persists throughout various clinical subtypes, including relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS), primary progressive MS (PPMS), and secondary progressive MS (SPMS), which together account for over 85% of MS cases13. Given their central involvement in MS pathology, activated microglia and macrophages can serve as clinically relevant biomarkers of chronic neuroinflammation and disease progression.

Currently, there is no cure for MS, but several disease-modifying therapies (DMT) are approved, primarily for managing RRMS and SPMS, with only one Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved option for PPMS14. These treatments mainly work by modulating immune responses or depleting specific immune cell populations to reduce disease activity and slow clinical progression15. While no FDA-approved MS therapies directly target activated myeloid cells, a growing number of investigational treatments aim to address this gap. Moreover, several existing immunomodulatory therapies indirectly affect myeloid cells through changes in cytokine signaling and adaptive immune cell-mediated pathways4. Despite these advancements, PPMS remains particularly challenging to manage. The complexity and heterogeneity of MS – driven by multiple interacting immune cell types – makes selecting effective therapies difficult4. Compounding this challenge is the lack of specific in vivo imaging biomarkers for activated myeloid cells, which limits our ability to fully elucidate their role in neurodegeneration, stratify patients for trials of emerging microglia-targeting treatments, or monitor therapeutic responses.

Structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the current standard of care for diagnosing and staging MS lesions, as well as for monitoring treatment response16. While MRI is effective for visualizing structural changes, it lacks the molecular specificity needed to differentiate different immune cell subsets. As a result, MRI provides limited insight into treatment efficacy at the cellular level and may lead to suboptimal therapeutic choices, increasing the risk of continued CNS damage. Since activated myeloid cells are an early and persistent feature of MS and play a critical role in disease progression and remission, there is a critical need for non-invasive imaging strategies to specifically identify and track maladaptive myeloid populations and their functional phenotypes in the CNS of MS patients.

Positron emission tomography (PET) is a functional molecular imaging modality that has the potential to profoundly enhance our understanding of the in vivo roles of activated myeloid cells in MS. Unfortunately, the current selection of PET tracers for imaging innate immune activation is limited. The most widely evaluated PET tracers for visualizing activated myeloid cells target the translocator protein 18 kDa (TSPO)17,18. Despite providing valuable insights into the spatiotemporal dynamics of neuroinflammation in MS patients in addition to showing potential for predicting disease progression19,20, TSPO-PET imaging has several critical limitations, including its lack of cellular specificity (i.e., it is expressed on microglia, peripheral myeloid cells, astrocytes, and vascular endothelium, thus making interpretation of images challenging), unclear functional role in MS, and a genetic polymorphism in the human TSPO gene resulting in variable binding affinity across patients for all second-generation TSPO-PET tracers21. Moreover, recent post-mortem studies of MS brain tissue revealed that TSPO expression does not increase in activated cells but rather in the number of TSPO-expressing cells, underscoring its limitations as a reliable biomarker for myeloid activation22. While alternative PET imaging targets, such as colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R), cluster of differentiation molecule 11b (CD11b), cyclooxygenase-2 (COX2), triggering receptor expressed on myeloid cells 1 (TREM1), and P2Y purinoceptor 12 (P2Y12R), are being investigated as potentially improved biomarkers for specific in vivo tracking of innate immune activation23, none have yet been validated as effective clinical biomarkers for neuroinflammation.

To address this unmet need for a PET tracer that enables highly specific detection of activated myeloid cells24, we recently developed 18F-flurimedrimer (18F-FMD; previously known as 18F-OP-801), a fluorine-18-labeled synthetic fourth-generation polyamidoamine (PAMAM) hydroxyl dendrimer25,26. Fourth-generation hydroxyl dendrimers have been demonstrated to penetrate regions of a dysfunctional, but not healthy, intact blood-brain barrier (BBB), where they are quickly and selectively taken up by activated myeloid cells via fluid-phase endocytosis and rapidly cleared from tissue that does not contain these cells27–34. In preclinical PET imaging, we have demonstrated that 18F-FMD sensitively detects neuroinflammation induced by systemic sepsis in a lipopolysaccharide mouse model, with signal intensity correlating with the murine sepsis severity score35. Moreover, the synthesis of 18F-FMD has recently been optimized and approved for clinical use26, positioning this PET tracer as a potentially valuable tool for highly specific, functionally relevant, and non-invasive imaging of activated myeloid cells in patients with MS and other inflammatory diseases.

In this study, we evaluate the ability of 18F-FMD to non-invasively detect activated myeloid cells in an experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) mouse model at both presymptomatic and acute disease stages (Fig. 1). We demonstrate that 18F-FMD selectively accumulates in activated myeloid cells and sensitively tracks therapeutic modulation of neuroinflammation by fingolimod (FTY720), an FDA-approved small-molecule immunosuppressant, and H74DS3M8, a recently developed hydroxyl dendrimer-based receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor (referred to as “dendranib”). These findings establish 18F-FMD as a promising tool for in vivo monitoring of innate immune activation in the CNS and support its translational potential for evaluating therapeutic response and disease progression in neuroinflammatory disorders.

---

## Results

18F-FMD PET imaging enables early disease detection in EAE mice before symptom onset
We first assessed the ability of 18F-FMD PET imaging to detect and track activated myeloid cells in vivo in an EAE mouse model characterized by a sustained progressive disease course with persistent inflammation, demyelination, and axonal degeneration36–38. PET/computed tomography (CT) imaging was performed at presymptomatic (pre-EAE; score 0, no paresis/paralysis, ≥1 g weight loss in 24–48 h) and symptomatic (EAE; score 0.5–3.5, hindlimb paresis/paralysis) stages of disease, compared to naïve controls, 50 min after tracer injection (Fig. 2a). Clinical signs of EAE, which progress rostrocaudally from the tail to hindlimbs and forelimbs, began to manifest by day 12 and peaked by day 15 with an average disease score of 2.3 ± 1.2 (Fig. 2b and Supplementary Table 2).

In naïve mice, 18F-FMD PET signal was predominantly observed in the kidneys and bladder, reflecting the tracer’s urinary excretion pathway. Conversely, pre-EAE and symptomatic EAE mice exhibited visible increases in spinal cord signal (Fig. 2c, white arrow). PET image quantification confirmed elevated 18F-FMD uptake in pre-EAE mice compared to naïve controls in both the cervical/thoracic (0.69 to 1.02 %ID/g [percent injected dose per gram]) and lumbar (2.04–2.71 %ID/g) spinal cord regions (p<0.05; Fig. 2d). The signal increased further upon symptom manifestation in EAE mice, reaching 2.92 %ID/g in the cervical/thoracic and 4.71 %ID/g in the lumbar spinal cord (p<0.05; Fig. 2e). While no significant differences in 18F-FMD PET signal were observed in the brain during the pre-EAE stage, symptomatic EAE mice showed elevated tracer uptake in white matter-rich brain regions, particularly the cerebellum (0.29 to 1.05 %ID/g) and pons (0.29 to 1.06 %ID/g; p<0.05).

Following PET/CT imaging, mice were perfused with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) to remove residual tracer in the blood pool. Ex vivo gamma counting was then performed to validate in vivo PET findings in CNS tissues. Notably, in pre-EAE mice with no clinical symptoms, 18F-FMD signal in the lumbar spinal cord was significantly elevated compared to naïve controls (p<0.01; Fig. 3a). As the disease progressed, tracer accumulation markedly intensified, with symptomatic EAE mice showing a 2- to 4.5-fold increase in PET signal in the cervical/thoracic and lumbar spinal cords compared to pre-EAE mice, and a dramatic 9- to 12-fold increase compared to naïve controls (p<0.01; Fig. 3a). Additionally, tracer uptake in the blood pool of symptomatic EAE mice was significantly higher than in naïve mice (p<0.0001), with a trend toward significance in pre-EAE mice (p=0.29; Supplementary Fig. 3a). However, no significant differences were observed in peripheral organs such as spleen, which is known to exhibit fluctuations in immune cell populations like T cells, B cells, monocytes, and neutrophils during EAE39.

High-resolution autoradiography of lumbar spinal cords validated the in vivo PET and ex vivo gamma counting results. In naïve mice, 18F-FMD signal was minimal (Fig. 3b). In contrast, despite pre-EAE mice showed no clinical symptoms, they exhibited focal tracer uptake in regions corresponding to early immune cell infiltration. Strikingly, symptomatic EAE mice with hindlimb paralysis demonstrated even more pronounced tracer accumulation, forming punctuate hotspots that colocalized with multifocal mononuclear infiltrates and peripheral white matter demyelination in adjacent hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained sections, which are hallmarks of inflammatory lesions in this EAE model40,41 (Fig. 3c). Quantitative analysis of autoradiography supported these findings, revealing a 2.5-fold and 3.5-fold increase in tracer uptake in the spinal cords of pre-EAE and symptomatic EAE mice, respectively, compared to naïve controls (p<0.05; Supplementary Fig. 3b). Furthermore, CD68 immunohistochemical staining in a subset of mice from the same PET imaging cohort confirmed the presence of activated myeloid cells in the lumbar spinal cords of both pre-EAE and symptomatic EAE mice (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 4). Together, these results provide compelling evidence for the specificity and sensitivity of 18F-FMD PET in detecting neuroinflammation.

CSF1R dendranib is effective in reducing EAE disease severity
H74DS3M8 is a hydroxyl dendrimer, conjugated with eight dasatinib payloads, engineered to selectively target activated myeloid cells via fluid-phase endocytosis and inhibit CSF1R with high potency42,43. Hydroxyl dendrimers of this class are metabolically stable and are eliminated intact via renal clearance44–46. Kinase profiling revealed its sub-nanomolar potency against CSF1R, ABL tyrosine kinase 1 (ABL1), cluster of differentiation 117 (c-Kit), and cellular Src (c-Src), with minimal off-target activity against epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and platelet-derived growth factor receptor beta (PDGFRβ; Supplementary Table 3). In cell-based assays, H74DS3M8 inhibited proliferation in bellus verum 2 (BV2) microglial cells in a dose-dependent manner, with an IC50 of 343 nM at 52 h (Supplementary Fig. 1). Importantly, this effect on inhibition of proliferation was seen in the absence of cell death, differentiating the mechanism of action of H74DS3M8 from other CSF1R inhibitors whose primary mechanism is through microglial killing or depletion. Pharmacokinetic studies demonstrated sustained systemic exposure following both intraperitoneal (i.p.) and intravenous administration, supporting its suitability for in vivo applications (Supplementary Table 4). Noncompartmental analysis of sparse-sampling data revealed log-linear elimination kinetics with terminal plasma half-lives (HL_Lambda_z) of 3.44 h (i.p.) and 3.15 h (intravenous, i.v.), respectively (Supplementary Fig. 2), consistent with a clearance profile appropriate for therapeutic targeting of CNS inflammation.

To evaluate its therapeutic potential in a context of neuroinflammation and demyelination, we treated EAE mice daily with H74DS3M8 (60 mg/kg, i.p.). Disease severity was compared to vehicle-treated controls (4.4% [weight per volume] trehalose dihydrate/10 mM histidine via i.p. injection) and FTY720-treated mice (3 mg/kg via oral gavage; Fig. 4a). Treatment began at the presymptomatic stage on day 8 post-EAE induction, the earliest timepoint at which 18F-FMD PET imaging detected molecular changes in myeloid cell activation. By day 15, 100% of vehicle-treated mice developed mild to severe EAE symptoms (Fig. 4b). In contrast, only 52% of H74DS3M8-treated mice and 27% of FTY720-treated mice showed mild symptoms (e.g., tail weakness), with none progressing to severe EAE (e.g., hindlimb paralysis). Both treatments effectively reduced disease severity, with average scores reduced to 0.6 ± 0.9 (H74DS3M8) and 0.4 ± 0.6 (FTY720), compared to 2.7 ± 0.9 in vehicle-treated controls by day 15 (p<0.0001; Fig. 4b and Supplementary Table 5).

18F-FMD PET imaging sensitively detects therapeutic response of EAE mice to different MS therapies
To assess the ability of 18F-FMD PET to monitor the immunomodulatory effects of H74DS3M8 in vivo, we performed a treatment monitoring study comparing its therapeutic efficacy to FTY720 and vehicle control in EAE mice. On day 15 post-EAE induction, 18F-FMD PET imaging showed a marked reduction in spinal cord signal (white arrow) in both H74DS3M8- and FTY720-treated mice compared to vehicle-treated controls (Fig. 4c). Quantification of in vivo PET images revealed significant decreases in tracer uptake across multiple CNS regions, including the medulla (p<0.01), cerebellum (p<0.01), pons (p<0.05), cervical/thoracic spinal cord (p<0.01), and lumbar spinal cord (p<0.05), consistent with a reduction in innate immune activity. These results demonstrate that 18F-FMD PET imaging can sensitively detect the immunomodulatory effects of both treatments (Fig. 4d).

Ex vivo gamma counting and high-resolution autoradiography further confirmed in vivo PET findings. H74DS3M8- and FTY720-treated EAE mice showed significantly lower 18F-FMD signal in the cervical/thoracic and lumbar spinal cords, as well as blood, compared to vehicle controls. The cervical/thoracic spinal cords of treated mice exhibited 5- to 8-fold lower signal, while lumbar spinal cords and blood showed 2- to 3-fold decreases (p<0.05; Fig. 5a and Supplementary Fig. 3c). Autoradiography confirmed these results, with H74DS3M8 and FTY720 reducing tracer signal to near-naïve levels (Fig. 5b and Supplementary Fig. 3d), and H&E staining revealed significantly less demyelination in treated mice, closely resembling naïve controls (Fig. 5c). Immunohistochemistry staining for CD68+ cells in the same PET imaging cohort confirmed negligible presence of activated myeloid cells in H74DS3M8- and FTY720-treated mice, underscoring their efficacy in modulating neuroinflammation and potentially altering disease severity (Fig. 5c and Supplementary Fig. 4).

Flow cytometry confirmed therapeutic modulation of CNS and peripheral myeloid responses in EAE
To identify the immune cell subsets driving neuroinflammation and assess their modulation by therapeutic interventions in this EAE mouse model, we performed single-cell flow cytometry on spinal cord and peripheral blood samples from naïve, pre-EAE, vehicle-treated, H74DS3M8-treated, and FTY720-treated EAE mice (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Fig. 5). This approach enabled profiling of immune dynamics across disease stages and treatment responses. Tissues were harvested on day 8 post-induction for pre-EAE mice and on day 15 for EAE mice treated with H74DS3M8, FTY720, and vehicle at various disease stages (score 0.5–3.5, hindlimb paresis/paralysis), as well as from naïve mice.

Flow cytometric analysis revealed profound immune remodeling in the CNS of EAE mice compared to naïve controls. There was a dramatic reduction in the proportion of resting microglia (CD11b+CD45lowTMEM119+), which declined from 69.9% in naïve mice to 20.28% in EAE mice. In parallel, activated microglia (CD11b+CD45lowTMEM119−) expanded significantly, from 0.13% to 20.84%, representing a >160-fold increase and indicating a marked phenotypic shift. This transformation was accompanied by widespread infiltration of peripheral immune cells, including T cells (CD3+CD45+; 0.49% in naïve vs. 22.39% in EAE), infiltrating macrophages (CD11b+CD45hi; 0.88% vs. 37.53%), monocyte/dendritic cells (DC) (CD11b+CD45hiLy6G−; 1.01% vs. 17.42%), and neutrophils (CD11b+CD45hiLy6G+; 0.99% vs. 13.64%) (all comparisons p<0.0001; Fig. 6b). Collectively, these data reveal a profound shift from a predominantly homeostatic microglial environment to a highly inflammatory landscape, with infiltrating macrophages emerging as the most abundant immune cell type within the CNS of EAE mice.

Prior to symptom onset, pre-EAE mice showed a substantial reduction in resting microglia (28.24% vs. 69.86% in naïve; p<0.0001) in the spinal cord, alongside an early expansion of activated microglia (1.32% vs. 0.13% in naïve), suggesting that innate immune activation precedes peripheral immune infiltration and may play a key initiating role in EAE pathogenesis. Notably, B cells (CD19+CD45+) remained absent from the CNS across all groups and stages, indicating a minimal role of B cells in this model. In the periphery, a parallel pattern of immune activation was observed: circulating myeloid cells increased significantly (p<0.05; Fig. 6c), and T cells underwent a transient expansion during the preclinical phase, suggesting early systemic priming. B cells in blood modestly declined during the pre-EAE stage and returned to baseline levels during acute disease, mirroring levels seen in naïve mice.

Building on this data, we next evaluated the therapeutic potential of H74DS3M8 in modulating immune cell populations and compared its effects to the established immunomodulator FTY720. Both treatments significantly reduced pathogenic myeloid populations in the CNS and peripheral blood of EAE mice, including activated microglia, infiltrating macrophages, and monocytes (p<0.01; Fig. 6b, c). H74DS3M8 also markedly suppressed CNS-infiltrating T cells, DCs, and neutrophils, and decreased both T and B cell frequencies in the circulation. FTY720 similarly inhibited T cell infiltration into the CNS and significantly reduced circulating monocytes, neutrophils, and B cells (p<0.001). To further characterize the functional impact of treatment, we analyzed macrophage polarization states. Both therapies significantly decreased the proportion of pro-inflammatory M1-like microglia/macrophages (CD11b+CD45+CD86+; p<0.0001; Supplementary Fig. 6).

18F-FMD is selectively taken up by activated myeloid cells in EAE mice
To investigate the specific cell populations that endocytose 18F-FMD and thus gain an understanding of what the signal in our 18F-FMD PET scans truly represent, we used Cy5-labeled generation-4 hydroxyl dendrimer (Cy5-HD), a fluorescent analog that closely mirrors the structure, size, and uptake mechanism of 18F-FMD. Cy5-HD was administered intraperitoneally to all experimental groups 24 h prior to tissue collection for flow cytometry analysis. Quantitative analysis revealed a significant increase in Cy5-HD+ myeloid populations, including infiltrating macrophages, activated microglia, neutrophils, and monocyte/DCs, in both the spinal cord and peripheral blood of pre-EAE and symptomatic EAE mice compared to naïve controls (p<0.001, Fig. 7). Among microglia, Cy5-HD uptake was more than 9-fold higher in cells with a pro-inflammatory, activated phenotype compared to resting microglia, which showed negligible uptake (Supplementary Fig. 7). T cells and B cells lacked Cy5-HD uptake, further supporting the tracer’s specificity for activated myeloid subsets.

Following therapeutic intervention, Cy5-HD+ myeloid populations were markedly reduced by up to 19-fold in infiltrating macrophages and 46-fold in activated microglia, highlighting the ability of both treatments to suppress pro-inflammatory innate immune activity (Fig. 7). These findings align with previously published findings demonstrating the selective accumulation of hydroxyl dendrimers in activated myeloid cells under inflammatory conditions27–29. Notably, the spatial and temporal distribution of Cy5-HD+ cells observed by flow cytometry closely mirrored the trends captured by in vivo PET imaging, ex vivo gamma counting, and autoradiography. PET signal intensity decreased 2- to 2.5-fold following treatment, paralleling the observed reductions in Cy5-HD+ myeloid populations.
